title.en: The Diving-Bird Creation: God and the Devil in Slavic Cosmogony
title.zh: 斯拉夫潛水鳥創世：神與魔之潛深取土

region.en: Dnieper region / Carpathians (symbolic pin at Kiev)
region.zh: 第聶伯河流域／喀爾巴阡山（象徵性定位於基輔）

texts.period: Recorded 19th c. in East-Slavic and South-Slavic folk collections (Afanasyev, Dragomanov); apocryphal strata from medieval Church Slavonic manuscripts

source.work: A. N. Afanasyev, Poetic Views of the Slavs on Nature (1865-69); W. R. S. Ralston, Songs of the Russian People, London 1872 (public domain); M. Dragomanov collections

summary.en: Before land, God commands the Devil (Satanael) diving under the primordial sea to bring up sand; the Devil hides a mouthful in his cheek, and God blesses the earth so it grows — bursting the Devil's cheek; the sand becomes the world, and the stolen bit becomes the mountains, marshes, and all the crooked places.
summary.zh: 太初無陸，神遣魔（薩塔那埃爾）潛入原初之海取沙；魔藏沙於腮中隱而不報，神祝土使長，爆其腮——所取之沙成世界，所竊之沙成山嶺、沼澤與一切崎嶇之地。

sensitivity.note: Folk cosmogony recorded in 19th-c. ethnography; modern Rodnovery (Slavic neo-pagan) communities claim heritage.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of the East-Slavic folk version (Afanasyev/Ralston 1872): 'The Lord said to Satanael: Dive into the sea and bring me a handful of earth with the words In the name of the Lord. The devil dove but forgot the words, brought earth, and God spread it on the water — and it grew.' Not verbatim.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of the East-Slavic folk version (Afanasyev/Ralston 1872); not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of the Ukrainian/Carpathian variant: The devil hid earth in his mouth to make his own world, but the earth grew and grew in his cheek until it burst — and from the stolen earth came the mountains and marshes and thorns; so God's earth is level and good, and the crooked places are the devil's theft. Not verbatim.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of the Ukrainian/Carpathian variant; not verbatim.

texts.language: East Slavic (Ukrainian/Belarusian/Russian dialects) and South Slavic dialects
texts.canonical_translation: W. R. S. Ralston, Songs of the Russian People, London 1872 (public domain); Louis Leger, La mythologie slave, Paris 1901 (public domain)

narrative.en:
Slavic pagan mythology survives in fragments — no pre-Christian Slavic text exists — but a cosmogony of extraordinary consistency was collected from oral tradition across the Slavic world in the 19th century, blended with apocryphal Church legend.

BEGINNING: THE WATERS AND THE TWO DIVERS. Before the world there is only water, with God (or in the apocryphal versions, the old god riding the waters in a boat? in the Russian versions: God walks on the sea) and his companion the Devil (Satanael, dyavol) swimming beneath. God commands the Devil to dive to the bottom and bring up a handful of earth 'with the words: In the name of the Lord'. The Devil — proud, and intending to make a world of his own — dives twice and fails (in some versions he is blocked by a voice: 'the bottom of the sea is mine'); the third time he takes the earth but forgets the sacred words, and he also conceals a second mouthful of sand in his cheek for himself.

MIDDLE: THE GROWING EARTH. God spreads the obedient earth on the waters and blesses it: 'grow, thou earth' — and it grows until it fills the sea. The stolen sand in the Devil's cheek also begins to grow, swelled by God's blessing, until the Devil's cheek bursts; he spits the earth out, and it becomes the mountains, gorges, marshes, and thorny wastes — everything uneven in the world. In the Ukrainian and Carpathian tellings, the Devil is flung from heaven first (a Lucifier-parallel from the apocrypha), and the diving is his punishment or his last claim to creative power.

END: THE TWO-WORLDED LAND. The world is thus double-authored: God's earth — the level, fertile plain — and the Devil's earth — the mountains, rocks, and swamps. The narrative aitiologizes the landscape of the Slavic east (the endless plain against the Carpathian uplands), locates evil in the crooked rather than the deep, and grounds the folk dualism that scholars (Ivanov & Toporov) trace to the Bogomil heresy carried north from the Balkans: God creates through obedience and word; the Devil through theft and pride. In the South Slavic versions, God and Devil are brothers, and the Devil is called 'our elder brother' — a familial dualism.

FUNCTIONS. The narrative grounds Slavic folk geography (the plain as blessed, mountains as stolen), the ethics of speech (the forgotten words of power), and the apocryphal theology of the medieval Church Slavonic manuscripts; it is the standard frame within which the fragmentary pre-Christian storm-myth (Perun vs. Veles, cross-ref) is read, and its motifs fed 19th-century Romantic reconstruction — which modern scholarship treats with caution.
narrative.zh: 斯拉夫前基督教神話無文本存世，而十九世紀民間採錄之創世敘事高度一致，並與教會偽經傳說相融。太初唯水；神（或曰騎水之老神）與其伴魔（薩塔那埃爾）居於水上。神命魔潛底取土，且須誦『奉主之名』；魔兩潛而不得（水中聲言『海底屬我』），第三次取得，然忘聖言，且於腮中私藏一撮欲自造世界。神展土於水面而祝之：『長吧，大地』——土長滿海；魔腮中之沙亦受祝而長，腮裂乃出，化為山嶺、峽谷、沼澤與荊棘之地。世界遂為雙造：神土平沃，魔土崎嶇——釋東斯拉夫平原與喀爾巴阡山地之貌，亦立『崎嶇為惡』之俗信。南斯拉夫版本中神魔為兄弟，稱魔為『我等長兄』。功能：民間地理釋義、言語倫理（力言之忘）、中世紀偽經神學；學者（伊凡諾夫與托波羅夫）溯其二元論至巴爾幹鮑戈米勒異端。

functions: Aition of Slavic landscape: the blessed plain and the Devil's crooked mountains
Ethics of speech: creation by obedient word vs. stolen silence
Folk dualism traced to Bogomil influence (Ivanov & Toporov)
Frame for reconstructing the pre-Christian Perun-Veles storm myth

variants.name: East-Slavic (Russian/Ukrainian) versions
variants.text_tradition: Afanasyev's Poetic Views of the Slavs (1865-69); Ralston 1872
variants.summary: God walks the waters; Satanael dives; the cheek of stolen earth bursts — the fullest recorded family, with dozens of local variants across gubernias.

variants.name: South Slavic (Bulgarian/Serbian) versions
variants.summary: God and the Devil as brothers ('our elder brother'), sometimes with the Devil creating men from clay and God animating them — the Bogomil-tinged dualism at its clearest.

variants.name: Church Slavonic apocrypha (Tolkovaya Paleya)
variants.summary: The written antecedent: Satanael as God's elder son cast from heaven; the diving-creation absorbed into apocryphal Genesis — the literary layer behind the folk versions.

primary_sources.citation: Collected in A. N. Afanasyev, Poetic Views of the Slavs on Nature, Moscow 1865-69 (vols. 1-3); W. R. S. Ralston, Songs of the Russian People, London 1872 (public domain), section on cosmogony; M. P. Dragomanov, collections 1870s-80s.

secondary_sources.work: Vyacheslav V. Ivanov and Vladimir N. Toporov, 'The Slavic versions of the myth of the cosmic dive'
secondary_sources.citation: Ivanov & Toporov 1970s, in scholarly collections on Slavic mythology (Russian) — the dualist-source analysis.
Leger 1901, Paris (public domain) — the classical synthesis of Slavic mythic fragments.

source_urls.description: Internet Archive — Ralston, Songs of the Russian People (1872, public domain)

title.en: The Tain Bo Cuailnge: The Cattle Raid of Cooley

region.zh: 愛爾蘭康諾特克魯亨山（拉思克羅根）

texts.period: Recension I in the Book of the Dun Cow (Leabhar na hUidre, c. 1100, RIA MS 23 E 25); Recension II in the Book of Leinster (c. 1160, TCD MS 1339); oral strata c. 7th-9th c.

source.archive: Internet Archive (Faraday translation, 1904) / Royal Irish Academy (Leabhar na hUidre)
source.work: Tain Bo Cuailnge, trans. Winifred Faraday, The Cattle-Raid of Cualnge, London 1904 (public domain); modern: Thomas Kinsella, The Tain, Oxford 1969 (copyright)

texts.license: Public domain (Faraday 1904); Kinsella 1969 quoted only as summary (copyright)

summary.en: Queen Medb of Connacht, quarreling with her husband Ailill over wealth, invades Ulster to seize the brown bull of Cooley — the one treasure matching her husband's white-horned bull; the men of Ulster lie in their labor-pains curse until the seventeen-year-old Cuchulainn holds the ford alone against the province, killing friend and foster-brother Ferdiad at the ford, until the bulls themselves meet and destroy each other.
summary.zh: 康諾特女王梅芙與夫艾利爾爭財，舉兵入阿爾斯特欲奪庫利棕牛——唯一可匹其夫白角牛之寶；阿爾斯特男子盡陷產褥之詛，唯十七歲之庫丘林獨守渡口，力抗一省之兵，於渡口誅摯友與結義兄弟弗迪亞，終致二牛相鬥、同歸於盡。

sensitivity.note: Manuscripts are Irish national heritage (RIA, TCD); living Gaelic and Irish-language communities hold the tradition.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of Tain (Recension I): Medb gathers the men of Connacht and asks of each a fair fight; the men of Ulster are seized by the ces noinden (the pains of childbirth curse); Cuchulainn alone, not yet seventeen, takes up arms: 'I will hold the ford against them all.' Not verbatim.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Tain (Recension I); not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of the Ferdiad episode: Cuchulainn and Ferdiad, foster-brothers taught by the same woman-warrior Scathach, meet at the ford; each calls the other by the love of their training days; after four days of combat Cuchulainn casts the gae bolga under Ferdiad's armor — 'not I alone, but my friend was slain' — and carries grief from the ford. Not verbatim.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of the Ferdiad episode; not verbatim.

texts.canonical_translation: Winifred Faraday, The Cattle-Raid of Cualnge, London 1904 (public domain); Thomas Kinsella, The Tain, Oxford 1969 (copyright); Cecile O'Rahilly, Tain Bo Cualnge from the Book of Leinster, Dublin 1967 (copyright)

narrative.en:
The Tain is the central epic of the Ulster Cycle — a cow-raid that escalates into an apocalypse of single combat, told with a raucous humor and tragic gravity unique in medieval European literature.

BEGINNING: THE PILLOW TALK AND THE RAID. Queen Medb of Connacht and her husband Ailill compare possessions in bed and find them equal — except Ailill's white-horned bull Finnbennach, formerly Medb's own (he defected to the herd for human treatment). Medb resolves to match him with the brown bull Donn Cuailnge of Ulster; negotiation fails (an insult at the feast), and Medb summons the province — seven thousand? twenty-seven camps, with her allies (the exiled Ulsterman Cormac, the hero Fergus mac Roich) — while a curse keeps the men of Ulster helpless: Macha's curse, the ces noinden, has them seized with the pangs of childbirth for five days and four nights after each alarm. Only the seventeen-year-old Cuchulainn (Setanta, son of the god Lugh) — too young for the curse — is left; he takes up arms at the Ford of the?, with his charioteer Laeg, and holds the border alone.

MIDDLE: THE SINGLE COMBAT AND THE WARP-SPASM. The Tain's middle is a sequence of single combats at the fords (the tradition of the iomarbad): Cuchulainn defeats champion after champion — his boyhood feats recalled, his warp-spasm (riastrad) described in horrifying detail (the contortion that makes him unrecognizable, one eye swallowed into his head, his blood rising like a mast?). He slays the queen's warriors, the loneliest of them his own foster-brother Fraech, and the men of Connacht offer terms; Fergus negotiates a day-by-day pact. The climax approaches when Medb sends Ferdiad mac Daman, Cuchulainn's closest friend, trained with him by the woman-warrior Scathach in Alba (Scotland). The two meet at the ford of Ardee; four days of combat, each night healing the other with herbs and each morning weeping; Cuchulainn finally casts the gae bolga — the barbed spear thrown underfoot that opens inside the body — and Ferdiad dies; Cuchulainn carries grief from the ford: 'not I alone, but my friend was slain'.

END: THE BULLS' DUEL. Medb breaks the pact and invades; the Ulster men rise from their pains at last and converge; the brown bull of Cooley, seized by Medb's host, kills the white-horned bull in a monstrous duel across Ireland (carrying him on his back through the land, his pieces forming place-names — the aition of the province), then runs wild and dies — 'the brown bull's heart broke within him'. The province is devastated, the raid futile: Medb's own evaluation ('it was a good cattle-raid... only that the men of? ' — 'we have gained nothing'), and the narrative closes with its most famous frame: the poet Fergus reciting the Tain to the poet Senchan Torpeist, whose students resurrect it from fragments — the self-referential moment when the epic claims oral transmission as its authority.

FUNCTIONS. The Tain grounds the Ulster heroic ideology (single combat at fords; the boy-hero vs. the cursed province), the legal theology of honor-price (Medb's argument about equal wealth as the marriage contract), and the aitiology of Irish topography (bull-duel place-names); it is taught as the Irish national epic and studied for its layering (oral saga, 8th-11th c. composition, manuscript transmission in the Book of the Dun Cow and Book of Leinster).
narrative.zh: 梅芙女王與夫艾利爾枕上較財，惟夫之白角牛勝其所有；欲得庫利棕牛以配之，談判不成遂興兵。阿爾斯特男子盡中瑪哈之詛（產褥之痛五日四夜），唯十七歲庫丘林（神魯格之子）免於詛，與御者萊格獨守渡口，歷經單挑：其變形痙攣（riastrad）之狀可怖，連誅康諾特諸將。梅芙遣其摯友與同門（同師女戰士斯卡哈）弗迪亞；二人於阿迪渡口血戰四日，夜以草藥互療、晨起相泣；庫丘林終以腳下倒鉤槍（gae bolga）破其甲而殺之，扶屍而慟：『非獨我殺之，亦殺我友。』梅芙毀約入侵，阿爾斯特眾起；棕牛奪回，與白角牛鬥於全愛爾蘭，背負死敵而奔，碎為地名——牛心碎而亡。梅芙自評：『一場好劫，然所得無幾。』史詩以詩人費爾古斯向詩人森坎誦述《奪牛記》為結，自證口傳之權威。功能：阿爾斯特英雄意識形態、榮譽價之法律神學、牛鬥地名之地理釋義、以及口傳傳承之自我宣稱。

functions: Charter of Ulster heroic ideology: ford-combat, the boy-hero, the cursed province
Legal theology: honor-price and the marriage contract of equal wealth
Topographical aition: bull-duel place-names across Ireland
Oral authority: the epic's self-referential frame of transmission

variants.name: Recension I (Book of the Dun Cow)
variants.text_tradition: Leabhar na hUidre, c. 1100 (RIA MS 23 E 25)
variants.summary: The older recension: more archaic language, the Ferdiad episode in fuller form, and the Resignation? ('Divorce of Medb and Ailill') attached — the classicist's base text.

variants.name: Recension II (Book of Leinster)
variants.summary: Adds the preamble (the poets' recovery of the lost Tain from the Otherworld dead — Fergus reciting to Senchan) and rearranges episodes; the version behind most modern translations.

variants.name: Stowe and later recensions
variants.summary: Later continuous versions with prose expansion; evidence of the Tain's living recitation into the Early Modern period.

variants.name: Dindsenchas and place-name tradition
variants.summary: Independent place-name poems (e.g. of Ardee, of the fords) preserve the Tain's episodes as aitiologies — the topographical stratum of the tradition.

primary_sources.work: Tain Bo Cuailnge (Recensions I and II)
primary_sources.citation: Rec. I: Book of the Dun Cow (RIA MS 23 E 25, c. 1100); Rec. II: Book of Leinster (TCD MS 1339, c. 1160). Translations: Faraday 1904 (public domain); O'Rahilly 1967; Kinsella 1969 (copyright).

secondary_sources.work: Kim McCone, 'A Beginner's Guide to the Tain'
secondary_sources.citation: McCone 1984, Emania 1 — structural and legal analysis of the epic.
Kinsella 1969, Oxford University Press — introduction surveying the recensions and oral layers.

title.en: The Dainas: Sun, Moon, and the World-Tree of Latvian Cosmogony
title.zh: 《達伊納》歌謠：拉脫維亞創世中的日、月與世界樹

region.en: Latvia (symbolic pin at Kurzeme daina region)
region.zh: 拉脫維亞（象徵性定位於庫爾澤梅歌謠區）

texts.period: Oral tradition; collected by Krisjanis Barons, Latvju dainas (1894-1915, ~218,000 variants); dainas attested from 16th-c. collections onward

source.archive: Barons' Dainu skapis (UNESCO Memory of the World) / Internet Archive
source.work: Krisjanis Barons (ed.), Latvju dainas, Jelgava/St. Petersburg 1894-1915 (public domain); English: Uldis Balcitis; scholarly: Haralds Biezais, Die Hauptzuge der lettischen Religion, Uppsala 1975

summary.en: In the dainas the world is an arranged household: Dievs (God) rides across the sky estate; Saule (Sun) hangs her gold belt on the world-tree, her daughter is stolen by the Moon; the tree of life grows at the sea's edge with its roots in the waters and its crown in the stars — a cosmogony sung, not told.
summary.zh: 達伊納歌謠中，世界如一家宅：天神騎行天域，太陽女神以金帶掛於世界樹，其女為月亮所竊；生命之樹生於海畔，根入水、冠入星——此為以歌傳而非以述傳之創世觀。

sensitivity.note: Living Latvian tradition (Jani festival; Dievturiba modern revival claims heritage).

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of daina variants on the world-tree: 'The tree of life grew at the edge of the sea, its roots in the water, its crown in the stars; its branches bore? the girls came to it with silk ribbons' — the world-tree as gold-bearing tree (zelta koks) sung in hundreds of variants. Not verbatim.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of daina variants on the world-tree; not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of daina variants on Sun and Moon: Saule, the sun-goddess, hangs her golden belt on the world-tree and goes to rest; Meness (Moon) climbs and takes her daughter (Saules meita) — 'the moon took the sun's daughter for his wife' — and the gods? Dievs judges between them: the daughter is returned, and the sun and moon part ways across the sky. Not verbatim.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of daina variants on Sun and Moon; not verbatim.

texts.canonical_translation: Krisjanis Barons, Latvju dainas (1894-1915, public domain); English selections in Uldis Balcitis and in Vaira Vike-Freiberga's translations (copyright)

narrative.en:
Latvian mythology survives in the daina — a four-line trochaic song form of which Krisjanis Barons collected over 217,996 variants (Latvju dainas, 1894-1915; the Dainu skapis card-file is UNESCO Memory of the World). There is no prose cosmogony: the world is sung in thousands of fragments, and the cosmogony must be assembled from song.

THE ARRANGED HOUSEHOLD. The dainas image the cosmos as an estate (saimnieciba): Dievs, the sky-god, rides across it on horseback (or sledge), descending to the fields at sowing time; Saule, the sun-goddess, washes her horses in the sea, hangs her gold belt on the branches of the world-tree, and drives her wagon of light; Meness, the moon, travels the night roads; Auseklis, the morning star, keeps the threshold; and the Saules meitas ('daughters of the sun') work the golden looms at the sea's edge. The cosmos is domestic: gods are householders, and myth is choreography of chores.

THE WORLD-TREE. At the center stands the tree of life (dzivibas koks): the golden tree (zelta koks) growing at the sea's edge 'with roots in the water and crown in the stars', hung with the sun's belt, climbed by the daughters, flanked by the heavenly estate. Hundreds of variants describe it: a tree of gold, silver, and? a ship with a tree mast, a birch on the sea-stone — the Indo-European world-tree in its Baltic form, close cousin to Yggdrasil (cross-ref norse-creation-ymir) and to the Indian axis motifs.

THE SUN'S DAUGHTER AND THE MOON'S THEFT. The most cosmogonic daina cycle is the abduction: Meness, the moon-god, takes Saule's daughter as wife (or steals her from the golden tree); the quarrel goes to judgment — in some variants before Dievs, in others before the celestial assembly — and the sun and moon are separated, explaining the day-night alternation: 'the sun and moon went apart... the moon took the sun's daughter...'. In other variants the daughter is? the story is a wedding dispute rather than a theft — evidence that the dainas preserve the myth in ritualized fragments (wedding songs, morning songs) rather than a single narrative.

FUNCTIONS. The dainas ground Latvian seasonal ritual (Jani solstice festival; the sun's belt as ornament), the household ethics of the cosmos (chores, weaving, horse-washing), and the modern national revival (Barons' collection as national canon; Dievturiba's reconstruction of the pantheon; daina singing as UNESCO intangible heritage 2003? — the Baltic Song and Dance Celebrations). The cosmogony is sung, and its 'records' are variants — the deepest methodological challenge in Baltic myth studies.
narrative.zh: 拉脫維亞神話存於四行短歌『達伊納』，巴倫斯採錄逾二十一萬八千變體（1894-1915；其卡片櫃入選聯合國教科文組織世界記憶遺產）。無散文體創世史：世界以千萬歌之碎片唱出。宇宙如家宅：天神迪埃夫斯騎馬巡天，播種時下田；太陽女神索萊於海中洗馬，以金帶掛世界樹，駕光之車；月神梅內斯行夜路；晨星奧塞克利斯守門檻；太陽眾女於海畔金色織機織布。中心為生命之樹：金色之樹生於海畔，根入水、冠入星，掛太陽之金帶，為眾女所攀——與北歐尤克特拉希爾同源而異形。最具創世性之循環為『太陽之女被月所竊』：月娶（或竊）日女，諸神裁斷，日月分途——釋晝夜交替；或另釋為婚禮之爭，證達伊納以儀式碎片保存神話。功能：季節儀式（雅尼夏至節）、家宅倫理之宇宙觀、以及現代民族復興（巴倫斯採集、迪維圖里巴復興、波羅的海歌舞節）。

functions: Seasonal ritual: Jani solstice, the sun's belt, and the celestial household's chores
Cosmology as domestic ethics: gods as householders and workers
National revival: Barons' collection as canon; daina singing as living heritage
Comparative myth: Baltic world-tree against Yggdrasil and the Indian axis

variants.name: Barons' Latvju dainas (1894-1915)
variants.text_tradition: ~218,000 collected variants; Dainu skapis card-file (UNESCO Memory of the World)
variants.summary: The canonical collection organizing variants by motif and region — the primary record from which any Latvian cosmogony must be assembled.

variants.name: Lithuanian parallel (dainos and tales)
variants.summary: The Lithuanian cognate songs share the sun-daughter and world-tree motifs with different names (Saule, Menulis) — the Baltic comparative base.

variants.name: Dievturiba reconstruction (modern)
variants.text_tradition: Ernests Brastins, Dievturiba ceram? (1920s); modern Latvian neo-pagan practice
variants.summary: A modern reconstruction systematizing the dainas into a prose pantheon and liturgy — useful but interpretive; scholarship treats it as revival, not source.

primary_sources.citation: Krisjanis Barons (ed.), Latvju dainas, 6 vols., Jelgava/St. Petersburg 1894-1915 (public domain); cosmogonic motifs: Sun-daughter cycle, world-tree cycle, Dievs' estate cycle. Card archive: Dainu skapis (UNESCO Memory of the World Register).

secondary_sources.work: Haralds Biezais, Die Hauptzuge der lettischen Religion
secondary_sources.citation: Biezais 1975, Uppsala: Almqvist & Wiksell — the standard academic synthesis of Latvian mythic motifs.
Puhvel 1987, Baltimore: Johns Hopkins University Press, Baltic chapter — Indo-European framing of the daina motifs.

source_urls.description: UNESCO Memory of the World — Krisjanis Barons' Dainu skapis (Latvju dainas card archive)
